claim: Condensin complexes are one of the most abundant non-histone complexes on mitotic chromosomes.
source: Condensin complexes, one of the most abundant non-histone complexes on mitotic chromosomes (Cuylen and Haering, 2011; Hirano et al., 1997; Ono et al., 2003), are composed of two structural maintenance of chromosome (SMC) proteins (SMC2 and SMC4) bridged by a kleisin subunit (Barren/Cap-H for condensin I and Barren2/Cap-H2 for condensin II)(Cuylen and Haering, 2011; Hirano et al., 1997; Ono et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: It is difficult to interpret the results when condensins are depleted prior to mitotic entry using conventional depletion approaches.

claim: Inactivation of condensin I specifically during metaphase leads to over-compaction at the majority of chromosomal regions.
source: We find that inactivation of one condensin I specifically during metaphase leads to over-compaction at the majority of chromosomal regions.

source: We further demonstrate that upon condensin I cleavage previously separated sister DNA molecules undergo topoisomerase II-dependent re-intertwining and complete failure in chromosome segregation.

claim: All modified versions of Barren with TEV-cleavage sites are fully functional as they were able to complement the lethality associated with the Barren null allele BarrL305.
source: All versions are fully functional as they were able to complement the lethality associated with the Barren null allele BarrL305 (Bhat et al., 1996) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1b and data not shown).

claim: In vitro cleavage experiments reveal that all modified Barren proteins are efficiently cleaved by TEV protease.
source: In vitro cleavage experiments reveal that all modified proteins are efficiently cleaved by TEV protease (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Direct injection of TEV-protease into syncytial embryos allowed cleavage and the removal of chromosome-associated BarrenTEV within 8–15 min.
source: Direct injection of TEV-protease into syncytial embryos, in contrast, allowed cleavage and the removal of chromosome-associated BarrenTEV within 8–15 min (Figure 1b,c), enabling the analysis of the immediate consequences upon disruption of this complex.

claim: Injection of TEV-protease in early interphase embryos leads to complete failure of the subsequent mitosis.
source: Injection of TEV-protease in early interphase embryos leads to complete failure of the subsequent mitosis (which takes place within ~15 min in these embryos).
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Although chromosomes were able to condense upon nuclear envelope breakdown, centromeres display significant stretching upon microtubule attachment after TEV-protease injection.
source: Although chromosomes were able to condense upon nuclear envelope breakdown, centromeres, monitored by the Cenp-A ortholog Cid-EGFP, display significant stretching upon microtubule attachment (Figure 2, Video 1 and Video 2).

claim: Resolution of sister chromatids is completely impaired after TEV-protease injection, as chromatids appeared as a fused chromatin mass or display very thick bridges during the attempted anaphase.

claim: The results from TEV-protease injection are in accordance with previous findings for condensin I depletion.

claim: Injection of buffer causes no change in the distance between centromeres.

evidence: This is a finding from the experiments shown in Figure 3, Video 3 and Video 4.

claim: TEV protease injection in strains containing solely TEV-cleavable Barren results in rapid separation of centromeres that appear to stretch towards the poles, leaving behind the majority of the chromatin mass.
source: Whereas injection of buffer causes no change in the distance between centromeres, TEV protease injection in strains containing solely TEV-cleavable Barren results in rapid separation of centromeres, that appear to stretch towards the poles, leaving behind the majority of the chromatin mass (Figure 3, Video 3 and Video 4).

claim: Condensin I is not only required for the establishment of a rigid structure at the pericentromeric domains prior to metaphase, but also for the maintenance of such organization.

claim: Injection of TEV protease in strains surviving only on BarrenTEV leads to an overall over-compaction of the entire chromatin mass, as evidenced by an increase in the mean voxel intensity and a decrease in both the surface area and the volume of the metaphase plate.
source: We found that injection of TEV protease in strains surviving only on BarrenTEV leads to an overall over-compaction of the entire chromatin mass, as evidenced by an increase in the mean voxel intensity and a decrease in both the surface area and the volume of the metaphase plate (Figure 3c,d).

claim: Injection of TEV protease in strains that do not contain TEV-cleavage sites does not result in any evident change in chromosome compaction relative to controls.
source: Injection of the protease in strains that do not contain TEV-cleavage sites does not result in any evident change in chromosome compaction relative to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), implying that chromosome over-compaction is specific of condensin I inactivation.

claim: Chromosome over-compaction is specific to condensin I inactivation.

These finding are consistent with the idea that metaphase chromosome structure is organized as a chromatin network resultant from self-entanglements of DNA strands, as initially proposed by biophysical studies on isolated chromosomes (Kawamura et al., 2010).

claim: Upon condensin I removal, creation of new links between previously separated DNA strands leads to their increased proximity, which may underlie the observed increase in chromosome compaction.

claim: Condensin I displays significant turn-over on mitotic chromosomes.
